concepts.title: Toy models (TSTMTCTMI)
concepts.one_liner: A toy model is the simplest possible version of a problem that still captures its main idea.
concepts.content:
A toy model is "the simplest toy model that captures the main idea" (TSTMTCTMI). Simple toy models help build intuition about what matters, which provides a significant advantage in research. 

For example, the color constancy problem involves estimating surface reflectance colors from the product of surface reflectance and an unknown illuminant spectrum. A toy model for this is estimating scalars $a$ and $b$ from their product $y = a \times b$. This simple problem allows one to think through loss functions and Bayesian decision theory.

(see figure: A toy model for the color constancy problem: $y = a \times b$. The plot shows the possible solutions for $a$ and $b$ when $y=1$.)

Another example is using a single bump as a proxy for complicated shaded surfaces. Having the intuitions gained from working with toy problems allows you to figure out what will work by thinking it through with the model.
concepts.motivation_md: Complex research problems often have too many variables to build immediate intuition. Toy models strip away non-essential details, allowing researchers to test logic and decision-making frameworks in a manageable environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Use the simplest model possible that still captures the core problem (TSTMTCTMI).

concepts.title: Parable of the two students
concepts.one_liner: Strong researchers explore small variations around a failed proposal to find a solution that actually works.
concepts.content:
In this parable, a weak and a strong graduate student are both asked by their advisor to try a particular approach to a research problem. The weak student does exactly what the advisor asked; when the solution fails, the student simply reports that failure. The strong student starts with the advisor's request but, upon seeing it doesn't work, looks within an epsilon ball of the original proposal to find what does work and reports that successful solution.

(see figure: The parable of the two students.)
concepts.motivation_md: This parable illustrates the difference between passive execution and active problem-solving. It encourages students to take agency and use their advisor's suggestions as a starting point rather than a rigid boundary.
concepts.recap_md: - Don't just report failure if an advisor's specific suggestion doesn't work.

concepts.title: Independent thinking vs. literature review
concepts.one_liner: Balance the freedom of thinking others are off-track with the necessity of knowing the existing literature.
concepts.content:
Sometimes it is useful to think that everyone else is completely off-track, as this allows you to pursue directions no one else is doing. When doing so, it is best to remain humble in communication, perhaps saying, "Oh, I just thought I'd try out this direction."

Conversely, it is also useful to remember that many smart people have worked on related problems and recorded their results. You should avoid being caught flat-footed by a large body of closely related literature that you are unfamiliar with.
concepts.motivation_md: Researchers must balance two extremes: being so influenced by existing work that they can't innovate, and being so isolated that they reinvent the wheel or ignore known pitfalls.
concepts.recap_md: - Use independent thinking to explore unique directions others might ignore.

concepts.title: Personal branding and reputation
concepts.one_liner: Build a personal brand by consistently producing great work and playing to your specific strengths.
concepts.content: In research, you have a brand: yourself. You should aim to build positive impressions—that you do great work, have good ideas, give great talks, and write wonderful software. Promote your brand by consistently behaving in the way you would like to be perceived. Additionally, cultivate and play to your specific strengths, whether those include being broad, creative, a great implementer, or skilled at theory.
concepts.motivation_md: A researcher's reputation (or 'brand') affects their opportunities for collaboration, funding, and employment. Consciously cultivating strengths helps a researcher stand out in a competitive field.
concepts.recap_md: - Consistently behave in the way you want to be perceived by the community.

concepts.title: Communication with your research advisor
concepts.one_liner: Maintain active and insistent communication with your research advisor.
concepts.content: Do not hide from your advisor. It is important to talk regularly. Advisors often appreciate it when students track them down and insist on meeting, especially if the advisor has been busy or traveling.
concepts.motivation_md: Regular communication prevents students from getting stuck for long periods and ensures that the advisor's expertise is being utilized effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - Avoid hiding from your advisor; insist on regular meetings to stay on track.

concepts.title: Slow down to speed up
concepts.one_liner: In research, taking the time to verify assumptions and understand algorithms deeply leads to faster progress than rushing through experiments without comprehension.
concepts.content: The advice "slow down to speed up" highlights a key difference between structured classroom learning and research. In research, there is no guaranteed correct answer or immediate feedback to identify mistakes. To handle this uncertainty, one should take things slowly by verifying assumptions and deeply understanding the program, algorithm, or proof. When conducting experiments, change only one variable at a time to ensure the results are interpretable. While this approach may feel slow, it prevents the lack of progress that comes from flailing around without understanding the system. (see figure: Research advice for a bumper sticker.)
concepts.motivation_md: Research lacks the clear structure and immediate feedback of coursework, making careful, methodical verification essential to avoid getting lost in complex, unidentifiable errors.

concepts.title: Reporting failures and progress effectively
concepts.one_liner: Effective progress reporting involves narrowing down where a system fails and ruling out potential causes rather than simply stating that it does not work.
concepts.content: When reporting issues, avoid simply stating that a system "doesn't work." Instead, identify the specific step where the failure occurs and demonstrate that previous steps are functioning as expected. Effective reporting includes ruling out specific causes and analyzing why a particular instance fails or if the issue is categorical. If a solution isn't immediate, try to create a simpler case that does work or a case that fails more dramatically to better understand the system's limits. Progress in research includes showing why something doesn't work, simplifying tasks, or spending time reading to build necessary understanding.
concepts.motivation_md: Precise failure reporting accelerates debugging and collaboration by allowing mentors and peers to focus on specific, isolated problems rather than the entire system.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Isolate failures to specific steps and provide evidence of where the system still functions correctly. , - Use simplified cases or extreme failure examples to probe the boundaries of the problem. , - Define progress broadly to include learning why a method fails or gaining necessary theoretical background. ]

concepts.title: Hard work and work-life balance in research
concepts.one_liner: Success in graduate-level research is driven by sustained hard work and a passion for the problem rather than just innate intelligence.
concepts.content: In graduate school, hard work is often what distinguishes successful researchers, as most peers are already highly intelligent. Similar to great athletes, the best researchers are often those who dedicate the most time to their practice. However, it is equally important to maintain a sustainable pace and a healthy work-life balance to protect the time needed for high-quality research. The most effective way to sustain this effort is to choose a research topic you love; if you enjoy the work, the necessary time and effort follow naturally.
concepts.motivation_md: Research is a marathon that requires consistent effort over long periods; understanding the role of persistence and passion helps students manage the transition from competitive schooling to open-ended discovery.

concepts.title: Steering and time management
concepts.one_liner: Steering involves periodically stepping back from hard work to ensure that efforts are being directed toward the right research problems.
concepts.content: While hard work provides the "motor" for research, "steering" provides the rudder. Steering means stepping back periodically to evaluate whether you are working on the right problems. Hard work alone is insufficient if the effort is misdirected. Utilizing time management strategies can be highly beneficial in learning how to prioritize and solve the most impactful problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Without periodic evaluation, a researcher might spend significant effort on low-impact or irrelevant tasks; steering ensures that hard work translates into meaningful progress.
